existing.description_long: In February 2025, Trump fired Hampton Dellinger, head of the Office of Special Counsel — the federal agency specifically created to protect government whistleblowers from retaliation. Dellinger, appointed by Biden in 2024 and confirmed by the Senate to a five-year term, sued, calling his removal unlawful. U.S. District Judge Amy Berman Jackson temporarily reinstated him on February 10, and on March 2 ruled his firing unlawful and issued a permanent injunction, finding Trump had violated federal law. The Trump administration rushed to appeal. The firing was widely interpreted as an attempt to eliminate the very agency that could shield employees reporting misconduct from retaliation, effectively clearing the way for agencies to punish internal dissenters without oversight. It followed a broader pattern of retaliatory action — including EPA firing at least 8 employees who signed a dissent letter in August 2025, and FEMA placing 21 employees on leave after they cosigned a critical open letter.

existing.description_long: On January 20, 2025, his first day back in office, Trump signed Executive Order 14160 declaring that children born in the United States to parents unlawfully or temporarily present were not entitled to citizenship — directly contradicting the 14th Amendment's Citizenship Clause and 128 years of settled law since Wong Kim Ark (1898). Federal judges across the country immediately blocked enforcement. The Trump administration ultimately asked the Supreme Court to weigh in, framing it as a dispute over nationwide injunctions. In June 2026, the Supreme Court struck down the order 6-3 in Trump v. Barbara, with Chief Justice John Roberts writing that children born on American soil are citizens at birth. Three justices — Alito, Gorsuch, and Thomas — would have upheld Trump's restrictions.

existing.description_long: In October 2022, the Justice Department subpoenaed Kash Patel to testify before a federal grand jury investigating classified documents at Mar-a-Lago — documents the FBI seized in an August 2022 search that recovered over 100 files bearing classification markings, including top-secret material. Patel initially refused to testify, invoking his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination. A federal judge then ordered him to testify under a grant of limited immunity from prosecution; he complied on November 3, 2022. He had told Breitbart in May 2022 that Trump had declassified whole sets of materials and that the White House counsel had simply failed to generate paperwork — a legally untenable position rejected by courts and national security law experts.

original_title: Trans Prisoners Transferred to Wrong-Gender Facilities

existing.title: Trans Prisoners Transferred to Wrong-Gender Facilities
existing.description_short: Trans Prisoners Transferred to Wrong-Gender Facilities
existing.description_long: EO 14168, signed January 20, 2025, directed the Attorney General to ensure 'males are not detained in women's prisons' and prohibited federal funds from covering gender-affirming care for inmates, immediately disrupting established Bureau of Prisons (BOP) protocols. A February 21, 2025 BOP memo ordered staff to refer to inmates by pronouns 'corresponding to their biological sex' and banned gender-affirming clothing, cosmetics, and wigs; a second memo one week later banned hormone therapy and surgeries. U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth issued multiple emergency injunctions beginning February 4, 2025, blocking transfers of named plaintiffs, but a DOJ official on February 18 directed BOP to begin moving all remaining transgender women to men's facilities not covered by the injunctions. An internal BOP memo obtained by the Marshall Project confirmed six transgender women and one transgender man were moved to facilities inconsistent with their gender identity. Incarcerated women who were transferred reported living in constant fear of sexual assault in men's prisons.

original_title: Trump Calls for Impeachment of Judge Boasberg After Deportation Ruling

existing.title: Trump Calls for Impeachment of Judge Boasberg After Deportation Ruling
existing.description_short: Trump Calls for Impeachment of Judge Boasberg After Deportation Ruling
existing.description_long: On March 18, 2025, President Trump escalated his attack on U.S. District Judge James Boasberg by explicitly calling for his impeachment on Truth Social, posting that the judge should be removed from the federal bench for blocking deportations under the Alien Enemies Act. This was a historically rare and constitutionally alarming call — federal judges hold lifetime appointments specifically to insulate them from political pressure, and calling for impeachment over a routine adverse ruling struck at the foundation of judicial independence. Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts issued a rare public statement defending the independence of the judiciary and rejecting impeachment as a response to unpopular rulings — the first time Roberts had directly rebuked a sitting president over judicial independence in the modern era. The episode drew comparisons to authoritarian leaders who have dismantled independent judiciaries in Hungary, Poland, Turkey, and Venezuela. Constitutional scholars warned that normalizing impeachment threats over legal rulings would permanently chill judicial independence.

original_title: Executive Orders Targeting Law Firms That Opposed Trump

existing.title: Executive Orders Targeting Law Firms That Opposed Trump
existing.description_short: Executive Orders Targeting Law Firms That Opposed Trump
existing.description_long: In March 2025, Trump signed executive orders against at least two major law firms that had represented clients opposing him or participated in his prosecutions. On March 6, an order against Perkins Coie — which had represented Hillary Clinton in 2016 — suspended the security clearances of all firm employees, directed federal agencies to terminate contracts, and launched a government-wide investigation of large law firms' diversity practices. On March 14, a nearly identical order targeted Paul Weiss because a former partner had brought a pro bono suit related to January 6 defendants. The orders blocked firm employees from entering federal buildings and directed agencies to require contractors to disclose any business with the targeted firms. A federal judge temporarily blocked the Perkins Coie order. Legal experts condemned both orders as a chilling use of executive power to punish lawyers for their clients' identities and associations, threatening access to justice and the independence of the legal system from political retaliation.

original_title: Melania's Plagiarized RNC Speech: Michelle Obama's Words, MAGA Packaging

existing.title: Melania's Plagiarized RNC Speech: Michelle Obama's Words, MAGA Packaging
existing.description_short: Melania's Plagiarized RNC Speech: Michelle Obama's Words, MAGA Packaging
existing.description_long: On July 18, 2016, Melania Trump delivered what was billed as a personally crafted prime-time speech at the Republican National Convention in Cleveland — except large passages were lifted nearly verbatim from Michelle Obama's 2008 Democratic National Convention address. Melania had told NBC's Today Show that she wrote the speech with as little help as possible. Side-by-side comparisons showed that lines including your word is your bond and you do what you say and keep your promise and the only limit to your achievements is the strength of your dreams and your willingness to work for them were direct mirrors of Obama's speech. Campaign manager Paul Manafort initially denied any plagiarism on CNN. Days later, the Trump campaign admitted that a staff writer, Meredith McIver, had included fragments from Obama's speech after Melania read them approvingly over the phone. McIver offered to resign; Trump declined. No disciplinary action was taken, and no substantive apology was made to Michelle Obama.

original_title: Trump Fires NLRB, MSPB, and FTC Members Without Cause

existing.title: Trump Fires NLRB, MSPB, and FTC Members Without Cause
existing.description_short: Trump Fires NLRB, MSPB, and FTC Members Without Cause
existing.description_long: In late January and early February 2025, Trump fired Gwynne Wilcox from the National Labor Relations Board, Cathy Harris from the Merit Systems Protection Board, and Alvaro Bedoya and Rebecca Kelly Slaughter from the Federal Trade Commission — all without cause, in direct violation of federal statutes that permit removal only for neglect of duty or malfeasance in office. These multi-member independent agencies were created by Congress with for-cause removal protections upheld by the Supreme Court for 90 years under Humphrey's Executor v. United States (1935). Acting Solicitor General Sarah Harris formally informed Congress in February 2025 that the DOJ would no longer defend the constitutional validity of these protections. The Supreme Court, in a 6-3 emergency stay in Trump v. Wilcox (May 2025), allowed the firings to proceed pending full review — with Justice Kagan's dissent warning the majority had allowed Trump to overrule Humphrey's by fiat and signaled the eventual overturn of a foundational check on presidential power.
